explanation:
**What the grids are made of.** Every input has a full-length wall of colour 5 along one edge (right edge in pair 1, bottom in pair 2, left in pair 3, top in the test), plus a few short straight segments lying parallel to that wall (vertical segments when the wall is vertical, horizontal when it is horizontal). The segments sit at different distances from the wall.

**What happens.** Each segment is swept toward the wall: the whole strip between the segment and the wall is filled with the segment's colour, giving a rectangle whose width is the segment's length and which runs right up to (but not over) the wall. The fact sheet confirms this: in pair 1 colour 7 (at x=2) gets 13 cells added rightwards in rows 8–10 ending next to colour 5; colour 3 at x=6 gets 9 cells per row; colour 2 at x=11 gets 4.

**Overlaps.** The rectangles overlap, so the order matters. In pair 1 row 7, the 7-strip (rows 7–10) and the 3-strip (rows 4–7) share row 7: the output shows 7 only for x=2..5 and 3 from x=6 on, i.e. the 3-rectangle sits on top. Colour 3 starts closer to the wall than 7. In pair 3 rows 5–6, the 3 (x=9) covers the 6 (x=13) region near the wall, and rows 10–11 the 2 (x=6) covers the 6 — again the segment nearer the wall wins. In pair 2, rows 11–14 show 3 (y=11) overwriting the 4 rectangle (y=3). So: paint rectangles from the farthest segment to the nearest; each nearer one overwrites.

**Applying to the test.** The wall is on the top row, so every segment extends upward to row 1. Painting order by distance from the wall, farthest first: colour 3 (row 15, x=2..10), then 2 (row 11, x=8..12), then 4 (row 7, x=0..3), then 8 (row 5, x=14..16). The 2-rectangle overlaps the 3-rectangle at x=8..10 and overwrites it in rows 1–11; the 4- and 8-rectangles happen to lie in columns of their own but are painted with the same rule.

**Construction in the program.** Locate the wall as a full single-colour non-background line on an edge (via `dividers`), which also fixes the sweep direction. Collect the other objects, sort them by decreasing distance to the wall, and stamp each rectangle from the object's bounding box to the cell adjacent to the wall, emitting after each stamp.
